opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most interesting open questions right now. Today most computer-use agents learn a kind of average way of doing things. They figure out how to book a flight or fill out a spreadsheet the way most people would. But the reason you'd delegate to an agent is that you want it done *your* way. You have preferences, shortcuts, and little rituals you might not even be able to articulate.

So I think it should feel less like programming and more like onboarding a new colleague. You don't hand a new teammate a giant spec. You show them once, they watch, they try it, and you correct them. Good agents should learn from demonstrations, from watching how you actually move through your tools, and then from lightweight feedback afterward. Something like "No, I always CC my manager on these," or "I prefer the aisle seat, and I never pay for the upgrade."

A big part of that is memory, and getting memory right is hard. The agent has to work out what's a durable preference and what was a one-off. If I picked a weird hotel once because a conference was nearby, that shouldn't become my identity forever. So there's a modeling challenge in separating stable habits from context-specific choices. There's also a product challenge in making that memory legible, so I can look at it and say, "Here's what it thinks it knows about me," and edit it.

Then there's the question of when it should ask versus act. Early on, I'd want it to check in more, almost like an apprentice. As it builds a track record and I trust it more, it can take on more autonomy. That trust calibration is something I think the field is still figuring out. Asking too often is annoying, and asking too rarely means it does something irreversible the wrong way.

And privacy matters a lot here. If an agent is learning from watching your screen and your workflows, that's an incredibly intimate dataset. People need real control over what gets observed, what gets remembered, and where it lives. Otherwise nobody will be comfortable letting these agents learn deeply enough to be useful.

So to me the ideal is an agent that starts out competent in a generic way and gradually becomes personal. Over weeks it stops feeling like a tool and starts feeling like it actually knows how you work.

r001.rationale: The response proposes teaching the agent by showing it how the user works, including learning from demonstrations of their actual tool use and correcting its attempts.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is that most of the "personalization" people imagine right now is the wrong shape. They picture a settings page, or a long onboarding interview where you tell the agent your preferences. That almost never works, because people are terrible at articulating how they actually do things. If you asked me to describe how I triage my inbox, I'd give you a clean little procedure, and it would be a lie. The real procedure lives in my hands, not in my head.

So the first principle is that the agent should learn mostly by watching, not by being told. The signal is in the demonstrations. When I do a task myself, the way I open three tabs before I even start, the fact that I always check the calendar before replying to a scheduling email, which Slack channels I ignore, how I name files. All of that is observable behavior, and it's way richer than anything I'd write down.

But then there's a second principle that I think people underweight, which is that the most valuable signal is the correction. When the agent does something and I go "no, not like that," and I fix it, that moment is gold. It's way more informative than watching me do a hundred tasks correctly, because it's telling the model exactly where its prior about "the generic way" diverged from "my way." So I'd want the system designed around making corrections cheap and natural. Not a thumbs-down button, but the agent noticing that I edited its draft, or undid its action, or took over the mouse halfway through, and treating that as a labeled example.

The third thing, and this is where it gets subtle, is the distinction between preference and context. Some of what looks like "my way" is a stable preference, like I always want terse emails. But a lot of it is situational. I write differently to my manager than to a vendor. I'm more careful on Fridays before a launch. A naive system will overfit on either side. It'll either flatten everything into one profile, or it'll treat every deviation as noise. So I think the model needs something like a hierarchy, where it's asking "is this a durable trait of this person, or a trait of this situation?" and it should be fairly conservative about promoting things to durable.

And then there's the question of how this is represented. I've gone back and forth on this. Weights-level personalization, like fine-tuning per user, is powerful but it's opaque and hard to audit. I lean toward some kind of explicit, inspectable memory, where the agent writes down what it thinks it's learned about you in a form you can actually read and edit. Partly for trust, because if the agent is going to act on my behalf with my accounts, I want to be able to see its model of me. But also because it creates a feedback loop. I can read "Karina prefers to CC her team on vendor emails" and go "actually no, that was one time," and delete it. That's a much better interface than hoping the gradient sorted it out.

The last thing I'd say is that there's a real tension between learning my way and knowing when my way is wrong. Sometimes I do things inefficiently out of habit. A good human assistant doesn't just mimic you, they occasionally say "I noticed you do this manually every week, want me to just automate it?" So I don't think the goal is pure imitation. It's more like the agent should be fluent in your way, default to it, and then have enough judgment to propose a better way without just unilaterally overriding you. Getting that balance right, honestly, is most of the problem.

r001.rationale: The response recommends learning from observed demonstrations, but it does not propose that a few demonstrations are sufficient to teach the user’s preferred workflow; it emphasizes corrections as more informative than watching many tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think they should learn by watching how you actually work, and then improve through your feedback. There are many ways to complete a task, and getting the right result doesn’t necessarily mean doing it the way you prefer. Maybe you always check a particular source first, or you want to review something before it gets sent.

So I’d want the agent to learn those preferences over time, with a way for you to inspect and correct what it thinks it knows. It should ask when something is ambiguous, but you shouldn’t have to explain your entire workflow every time. The interesting challenge is figuring out which behaviors reflect a lasting preference and which were just what made sense for that particular task.

r001.rationale: The response says agents should learn by watching how the user works and improving through feedback, but it does not specify using a few demonstrations to teach the preferred workflow.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they should learn from doing tasks with you. You might demonstrate something once, or the agent might try it and you say, “Actually, I prefer it this way.” That correction should carry forward, so you’re not explaining the same preference every time.

But there’s a distinction between learning your preferences and copying every click. If I take a weird detour because I can’t find a button, I don’t want the agent to memorize that. I want it to understand what I was trying to accomplish, which parts I care about, and where it has room to choose a better approach.

And that memory should be something you can inspect and change. It should feel like teaching a collaborator who gets better at working with you over time.

r001.rationale: The response says the user might demonstrate something once and describes learning from corrections, but it does not propose using a few demonstrations to teach the preferred workflow.
